## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dubbhiyamakkaṭajātaka* (Ja 174), translated in modern scholarship as *The Tricky Monkey*, is a narrative belonging to the canonical Pali Jātaka collection [Catalog]. According to its commentary's framing narrative, the Buddha related this story while dwelling at Veḷuvana in reference to Devadatta; upon overhearing the monastic assembly in the Hall of Truth discuss Devadatta's ingratitude and treachery toward friends, the Buddha explained that Devadatta had manifested identical behavior in previous lifetimes. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as a brahmin who draws water from a well for a thirsty monkey. Rather than expressing gratitude, the sated monkey makes faces at the Bodhisatta and, when chastised, insolently boasts of the shameless nature of monkeys and threatens to defecate upon him [Appleton 2010]. Naomi Appleton cites this tale as an illustration of how non-Buddhist or immoral characters in the Jātakas sometimes get the better of the Bodhisatta through their bad behavior, making the Bodhisatta appear foolish [Appleton 2010].
